issues.item: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile as a coherent pattern for a trauma-to-a-loved-one case: 'Cars hit by accident' suggests a specific road-traffic trauma cue, while 'Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place' implies separation/safety-context triggering. These could coexist, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content about separation, they look clinically mismatched within the trigger node.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory items describe vivid sensory re-experiencing of a frightening event, and the other appraisals emphasize unfairness and generalized vigilance, but nothing else suggests interpersonal betrayal. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one formulation, this appraisal would usually require supporting context (e.g. trusted person caused or enabled the harm), which is absent here.

The trigger profile is only weakly coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Workplace' as a major trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved-one trauma happened in the workplace or through occupational exposure, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other triggers (cars hit by accident, alcohol smell) imply a specific accident scene, making 'workplace' stand out as clinically questionable rather than part of the same trigger network.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Betrayal by someone I trusted' points toward an interpersonal trauma formulation, but the rest of the profile centers on sensory accident-related reminders and vivid perceptual memory. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this appraisal is difficult to integrate unless the loved one's trauma directly involved trusted-person betrayal, which is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node contains two items that are hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with each other. 'Constant Vigilance' implies an ongoing sense of current danger, but the formulation has no active Threat links and the rest of the profile is focused on accident-related reminders and vivid sensory memory rather than present threat. 'Self-Blame' is also difficult to fit with a loved-one accident trauma in this profile, because no other item suggests the patient had a causally responsible role in the event; combined with the injustice item, it creates a mixed appraisal pattern that lacks a clear coherent basis in the rest of the report.

issues.item: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, strong endorsement of both injustice/external blame ('nothing has been done about it') and self-blame for causing the event pulls in opposing directions and is difficult to reconcile as the same dominant appraisal without additional context. For a trauma to a loved one, these two appraisals can coexist in milder form, but selected together as core items they suggest conflicting attribution styles within the same node.

vignette:
Mele is a 71-year-old Tongan American police officer who has spent decades in patrol and community response, and she speaks about the night of the trauma with the blunt precision of someone used to writing reports, though the account still catches in her throat. Her husband had been driving home after meeting friends for dinner when another car crossed the median and struck his vehicle. Mele was not in the car, but she arrived at the scene before she could stop herself, having heard the dispatch and recognized enough details to know it might be him. What remains with her is not a full story in sequence but a set of brutally clear fragments: the crushed side of the car, the angle of the headlights against wet pavement, the smell around the wreck that she immediately registered as alcohol, and the sounds she heard at the roadside-metal settling, voices calling out, the strained noise of someone trying to breathe. Even now, when the memory comes, it comes as sharp pictures rather than thoughts, and with the pictures she sometimes hears those same sounds in her head. She says the memories are so clear and detailed that she can see the scene "like it's right in front of me again."

In the weeks afterward, Mele found that these sensory fragments seemed to prepare the ground for what would set her off in daily life. Because the memory is carried in images and sounds, certain moments hit her with unusual force. Driving past cars that have been hit in accidents can stop her cold; she does not just notice the damage but instantly sees her husband's vehicle superimposed on it. The smell of alcohol, whether on a person she encounters at work or lingering outside a restaurant, can bring back the roadside scene so vividly that she feels as if she is standing there again. Even hearing other officers or citizens talk about crashes can pull up the same visual flashes and the remembered sounds. As a police officer, she encounters all of this in exactly the places she cannot easily avoid: at roadside calls, in squad-room conversations after collisions, and in contact with intoxicated drivers. The memory seems to give those ordinary job moments a direct line back to that night.

What unsettles Mele most is where her mind goes next. When she sees a wrecked car or catches the smell of alcohol, she does not only remember; she immediately begins to judge herself. She has come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted, turning over small decisions from that evening and treating them as if they should have changed the outcome. In those moments she becomes certain she should have protected her husband and failed. A discussion about a traffic accident at work can leave her silent and rigid, not because she has nothing to say as an experienced officer, but because inside she is flooded with the conviction that she missed something, should have intervened earlier, should have prevented it. The trigger does not stay external for long; it lands as proof, in her mind, that she was not able to keep someone she loved safe.

Over months, this pattern has hardened. Passing damaged vehicles on patrol, catching alcohol on someone's breath during a stop, or overhearing talk about collisions can pull her back into the scene and into the same conclusions: that she failed, that her actions mattered in the worst possible way, that she cannot stop bad things from happening. That sense of helplessness has been especially painful because it cuts against the identity she built over a lifetime in policing. She has always been the person others relied on in emergencies. Now she finds herself dreading parts of the workday that once felt routine. She still goes in, but certain calls stay with her long after shift, and she has become more withdrawn with colleagues when crash reports are being discussed. At home, her husband's survival has not brought her peace; instead she watches him with an uneasy sense that safety can vanish without warning and that she cannot trust herself to prevent it.

By the time she seeks help, Mele is exhausted by how quickly the world can become the scene again. She wants relief from the pictures and the sounds that arrive so vividly, but just as urgently she wants help with the belief that she failed the person she loved most. What frightens her is not only remembering the crash. It is the possibility that every wrecked car, every trace of alcohol, every conversation about an accident will keep confirming what she has come to believe about herself-that when it mattered, she did not protect him, and that she may never feel capable of protecting anyone again.
